sections.overview: The buff-tailed bumblebee is a large social bee native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia. Its annual colony begins with one queen, grows through worker daughters, then produces males and future queens. People rear it commercially for crop pollination, and escaped colonies have established beyond its native range. European assessments still list it as widespread and Least Concern, a regional status that does not describe impacts after introduction elsewhere.
sections.identification: Adults have dense black fur, two golden-yellow bands and a pale abdomen tip. Queens measure about 20–22 millimetres, workers 11–17 and males 14–16; these British reference ranges vary among individuals. A queen’s tail is buff, while workers and males usually have white tails, sometimes with a fine buff edge. Workers can resemble the white-tailed bumblebee, Bombus lucorum; DNA markers distinguish the species more reliably than some field keys. The British field guide gives caste-specific body lengths of about 20–22 mm for queens, 11–17 mm for workers and 14–16 mm for males. It does not give a dependable body-mass range, and worker size varies substantially; no mass is inferred from length.
sections.habitat: The species uses gardens, parks, farmland and meadows where flowers and nest shelter are available. Queens often nest underground in abandoned rodent burrows, reusing their protected cavities. In Britain, queens emerge in late winter or early spring; workers appear about six weeks after a nest is founded.
sections.diet: Adults drink nectar for energy and gather pollen to nourish brood. Their short tongue works well on many open flowers but less well in long tubular blooms; they nevertheless forage as generalists across many plant species. Sometimes a bee pierces a flower’s side to reach nectar without touching its reproductive parts. On nightshades whose anthers release pollen through small pores, workers grip the anthers and vibrate flight muscles, shaking pollen loose into their hairs. The foundress feeds the first larvae; later, workers provision brood as the queen focuses on laying eggs. The nest contains small pots for sugary food, separate from clusters of brood cells. Unlike honeybees, these bumblebees vibrate flowers to release pollen from poricidal anthers. Pollen is also stored for the brood, but nectar and pollen reserves remain relatively small rather than providing a large winter stock.
sections.behavior: One mated queen founds the nest alone; her daughters become workers who forage, feed larvae and maintain it, while males mainly leave to seek mates. Colony size varies; British accounts give a broad range of 100 to 1,000 bees. Bumblebees lack the honeybee waggle dance; chemical and contact cues help coordinate activity. Workers can learn floral scents brought home by successful foragers. Flight muscles warm before flight in cool air. At the nest, queens and later workers also generate heat to keep brood warm.
sections.reproduction: In the usual temperate cycle, a mated queen spends winter in diapause and emerges when conditions allow nesting. Winter-active colonies have been observed in southern Britain, including urban parks and gardens. She lays eggs in a wax-lined nest and incubates them using heat from her flight muscles. Eggs hatch into larvae, which grow, spin cocoons and pupate; laboratory worker development averaged about 26 days from egg to adult, while field timing varies. The first workers take over much of the foraging and brood care. Later the colony produces males and new queens; after mating, the young queens enter diapause and the old colony normally dies.
sections.ecology: Foraging bees carry pollen between flowers, making them important pollinators of crops. Some crops benefit from the bee’s abundance and its ability to vibrate poricidal anthers, releasing pollen. Commercial rearing makes it a useful managed pollinator, but introductions can alter local communities. In Chile and Patagonia, surveys recorded introduced B. terrestris spreading as native B. dahlbomii retreated; competition and parasite spillover may contribute, though their relative roles remain unresolved. This regional case is distinct from the species’ widespread, Least Concern status in Europe.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment dated 14 July 2023 and published in 2025 lists B. terrestris as Least Concern in Europe and the EU27, citing its broad range and continued abundance. This regional status does not remove ecological concerns where commercial colonies escape and establish beyond the native range. A 2013 Patagonian survey reported rapid spread and a marked local replacement pattern involving native B. dahlbomii. A 2014 study detected parasites in introduced and native bees but said the evidence could not assign the decline to one cause. IUCN notes that climate and land-use change could affect the species in Europe in coming decades.
